Internal Incident Report: Gas Alarm, Cold Store 2, Harnsey Fish Works, Lantern Quay, Thornwick Sands

On a Thursday in July, the fixed ammonia-propane detector panel in Cold Store 2 registered its first high-level alarm at 1:48 a.m., with a peak reading of 38 percent of the lower explosive limit. The plant logged a call to the Gas Board reporting a suspected leak at 1:56 a.m. Fourteen workers were on shift. Night shift supervisor Odile Brandt heard the detector horn from the packing hall, ordered cold store staff out, and directed that the packing hall extraction fans be switched off. Brandt reported that no one raised symptoms with her at the muster point beside the ice plant. A Gas Board engineer assigned to the plant's incoming propane supply line reached the cold store doors before the fire brigade crew arrived on the quay. The brigade then established a cordon about 60 meters from the doors. Brigade crew members entered the cold store in breathing apparatus, took readings at the doorways, and declared it clear for re-entry. The detector panel fell below the alarm threshold at 3:05 a.m.

Two refrigerated trucks from Rennick Haulage were waiting at the loading dock when the alarm sounded. Both left the quay gate before 2:20 a.m. without their loads. The records disagree on how long the loading dock remained closed: the shift log cites about two hours, while the gate ledger indicates about four. Later that morning, frozen stock was transferred from Cold Store 2 to Cold Store 1. The operations team should reconcile the dock closure duration across both records and confirm the sequence of actions taken by the Gas Board engineer relative to the brigade's arrival.

Sources: Fixed ammonia-propane detector panel, Cold Store 2; Harnsey Fish Works Shift Log; Tomas Verrill, Thornwick Sands Fire Brigade crew commander; Thornwick Sands Gas Board Dispatch Record; Odile Brandt, night shift supervisor at Harnsey Fish Works; Rennick Haulage Gate Ledger

The grid supply to the Kestrel Ridge Observatory was lost at 00:58. The standby generator started automatically about twenty seconds later and ran for 38 minutes before shutting down at 01:36. The generator controller logged a stop event followed by a lockout state that required a manual reset at the generator panel. The cause of the shutdown remains disputed. The site engineer attributes it to overheating protection tripping after snow blocked the cooling air intake, while the night operator attributes it to low oil pressure protection tripping. The available records do not resolve this conflict, so the investigation must establish which protection function actuated and whether the other condition was also present.

Fuel exhaustion is ruled out as a contributing factor. The tank gauge read 61 percent at 01:00 and 48 percent at 02:00, with no sudden drop between 01:00 and 02:10. The generator's last routine test run took place eleven days before the storm and should be reviewed against maintenance practice.

The sequence of power loss in the control room is also inconsistently recorded. The night operator reported that the lights and dome drive went out while the battery-backed computers stayed on. The shift handover notes place the lighting failure first and the dome drive failure afterward, reversing the operator's sequence. The dome shutter had been closed at 00:50 because of incoming snow, before the power cut. The uninterruptible power supply serving the telescope control computers is rated for about 25 minutes of runtime. The site engineer walked from the staff cottage through the snow in roughly ten minutes and restarted the generator at 02:04 after resetting the lockout. The access road was closed by snow that night, which constrained external response.

Sources: Site engineer Talwen Pryce; Observatory night operator Imre Soller; Fuel tank level gauge record; Kestrel Ridge Observatory shift handover notes; Generator controller event log

At approximately 05:40 on a Tuesday in early March, freight train 7114 derailed on the Osterby curve of the Kestrel Branch. The train consisted of two locomotives and twenty-six cars, carrying two crew members in the lead locomotive who both walked away from the wreck without requiring medical transport. Engineer Dalia Ronk felt a sudden lurch through the cab floor and immediately applied the emergency brake. Following the emergency brake alert, Dispatcher Imre Voss contacted the maintenance office and immediately halted all rail traffic across the entire Kestrel Branch. A review of the wayside equipment confirmed that the detector had registered no overheated axle bearings on any car as the train passed. Approximately six miles prior to the incident, the wayside detector at Milepost 41 recorded the train traveling at 38 miles per hour, and the control log confirmed that the signal at the curve displayed a clear aspect. Out of the total consist, seven cars ultimately ended up off the rails, with three coming to rest on their sides. The maintenance crew utilized two heavy cranes to lift the overturned cars, and approximately 90 meters of track required total replacement. Normal operations and line reopening were successfully achieved at 21:30 on Thursday.

Sources: Brackenfell Rail Maintenance Report, Osterby Volunteer Ambulance Record, Wayside Detector at Milepost 41, Kestrel Junction Control Log, Engineer Dalia Ronk, Dispatcher Imre Voss

This internal operations review examines the flooding incident at the Vessel Hythe Land Registry following six hours of heavy rain on twenty-second October. Shortly after zero-one-thirty, approximately twelve thousand litres of water overflowed from a rooftop cooling tank for the air-conditioning loop, flooding the basement server room. During ground floor rounds, night security guard Ines Okafor heard water and investigated, while the basement water sensor array registered its first wet reading near the east wall at zero-one-thirty-six, with all six floor sensors reporting water by zero-one-forty-one. A flood alarm reached the guard console, and Okafor contacted registry IT systems lead Tomas Brandl and the Hythe Fire Service. Brandl remotely executed a database server shutdown from home, confirming that the nightly backup had finished at zero-one-fifty without any loss of title records. The sump pump started at zero-one-thirty-eight, but experienced a high-level fault at zero-two-zero-five that reduced output, running until zero-five-twenty. An arriving fire service engine crew used a portable pump before departing. Standing water eventually peaked between nine and fifteen centimetres, affecting only the two lowest rack-mounted storage units. Due to the incident, public counters remained closed all morning.

Sources: Registry Facilities Incident Report, Sump Pump Controller Log, Night security guard Ines Okafor, Hythe Fire Service Call Record, Basement Water Sensor Array, Registry IT Systems Lead Tomas Brandl

The fire at the cold-storage annex of the Veltrane Dye Depot on the Orsel Canal wharf began shortly after 04:00 on 22 October. Accounts of when the first alarm sounded differ. The annex smoke detector panel logged an alarm at 04:06, the brigade incident log records 04:11, and security camera footage shows the annex roller door glowing orange at its lower edge at 04:09. The panel recorded an alarm on zone 2 before any other zone reported, and its backup battery took over when mains power to the annex failed at 04:17. The first emergency call was logged at 04:12 by a passing canal barge pilot, who reported flames visible through the annex's upper vents. The first fire pumper left its station at 04:14.

Peak attendance also needs reconciling. The brigade log shows four appliances on scene, while the dispatcher's call record shows five. Firefighters drew water from the Orsel Canal using a floating suction hose, and the brigade closed the wharf road to traffic until mid-morning to allow hose lines to cross it. One firefighter was treated at the scene for a minor wrist burn and returned to duty.

On site that night, Imre Dallow was the only supervisor and led six warehouse staff out through the loading door. His headcount confirmed that everyone on the shift was accounted for in the yard within minutes of evacuation. Dallow stated that the annex's refrigeration compressors had been running normally during his 03:30 walk-round. Cameras on the north wharf lost power at 04:31, ending coverage of the annex's canal side and leaving a gap in the visual record for the later stages of the fire. The annex held about 40 pallets of powdered pigment and refrigerated dye concentrate. The insurance loss adjuster estimated that the annex roof collapsed entirely and that the main warehouse suffered only smoke and water damage.

Sources: Imre Dallow, Orsel Wharf Fire Brigade incident log, Canalside Logistics security camera system, Teodor Quill, Annex smoke detector panel, Pira Voss's call record

An operational incident occurred on a Thursday in May at the Lindqvist Textile Mill when a freight elevator in the Finishing Building trapped a cart operator. The car was traveling upward with a combined load of 1140 kilograms, which was well within the 1500 kilogram rated capacity, when the safety circuit issued a stop command at 1:26 p.m., halting the unit between the second and third floors. The operator used the intercom to contact security one minute later, prompting the finishing floor supervisor to respond to the third floor, maintain communication, and clear the remaining cargo using the stairs and a passenger lift. The elevator technician arrived on site 19 minutes past the hour, accessed the roof machine room, isolated the power supply, and manually released the brake to lower the car to the second floor, allowing the operator to exit unhurt after an entrapment duration of 25 to 40 minutes. Conflicting technical assessments subsequently emerged regarding the root cause, as the maintenance work order attributed the stoppage to an overspeed governor trip dating back to a March inspection, whereas the technician determined the issue stemmed from a worn door interlock contact on the third floor landing door. The unit remained tagged out of service until the safety circuit was fully reset the following morning.

Sources: Teodor Bram, Lindqvist Mill Elevator Controller Event Log, Imogen Pask, Lindqvist Mill Maintenance Work Order, Dorrel Vance, Lindqvist Mill Security Desk Log

This internal incident report details the mechanical failure of the Varnholt Swing Bridge that occurred on a Tuesday evening in early March. After the sailing barge Marl Heron passed safely, the harbourmaster ordered a vessel hold to close the channel for the evening. The bridge operator initiated the closing sequence, successfully lowering the road barriers on both approaches. However, the rotating span failed to seat properly, stopping fourteen centimetres short of the piers at 10:04. A second closing attempt was aborted after the span moved less than one centimetre and tripped the motor current limit. The operator immediately contacted the port engineer's on-call line, keeping the bridge closed to all road and foot traffic with the barriers down. At the east barrier, seven waiting vehicles and one cyclist were impacted, and pedestrians walked back along the eastern footway to the quay road. Additionally, buses were held at the Varnholt Green stop, and the number six service was diverted via the Quillon Ring Road, causing an approximate twenty-minute delay to the route.

Sources: Eskerlow Port Bridge Office Operations Log, Swing Span Position Encoder Record, Varnholt Parish Bus Depot Dispatcher's Notebook, Bridge operator Imre Valtonen, Harbourmaster Odile Brandvik, Cyclist Tobias Renwick

The main fibre link between Skerrin Isle and the mainland failed at 11:52 p.m. on a Tuesday in late October. The network monitoring system recorded a total loss of optical signal in a single reading, with no gradual decline beforehand, and no signal returned on the main link during the night. According to the monitoring system, the backup radio link began carrying island traffic at 11:53 p.m., one minute after the failure. The incident ticket, however, records the backup link as activated at 12:20 a.m., after the on-duty engineer opened the ticket, which was classed as priority two. This discrepancy between the two timestamps should be reconciled before the review is finalised. The backup link is rated at 20 megabits per second, far below the island's normal main-link capacity of 1,000 megabits per second, so services were substantially affected. The ticket lists a repair ship as requested from the mainland depot, but no arrival date has been confirmed.

The effects were felt across the island the following morning. The clinic's electronic patient records system was unreachable when the clinic administrator, Nessa Okonkwo, arrived at 7:30 a.m., and staff moved to paper forms for the 14 morning appointments. Card payments at the pharmacy counter failed, so only cash was accepted until the afternoon. At the school, IT technician Priya Venn reported that the online registration system would not load at 8:40 a.m., and video lessons for older pupils were cancelled because the backup link could not carry them. At the ferry office, online booking was unavailable for the first four of the six sailings, returning before the afternoon departures. The 9:15 a.m. sailing departed on time with paper tickets issued at the quay, using handwritten ticket forms prepared in advance. Harbour Master Tobias Reld reported that the sea was calm overnight, with winds below 10 knots, and that no vessels were anchored near the cable route after dark.

Sources: Corran Telecom incident ticket, Nessa Okonkwo, Harbour Master Tobias Reld, Skerrin Isle Ferry Office log, Corran Telecom network monitoring system, Skerrin Isle School IT technician Priya Venn

On a Sunday at Tessarine Bay Airport, Screening Line 3 experienced an operational disruption when the hold-baggage x-ray conveyor stopped following a motor overcurrent trip logged on the entry belt at 11:26:09. The system recorded a motor current of 31 amps against a rated 24 amps, and two additional trips occurred later that morning. The screening hall supervisor reported a grinding sound and about a dozen bags stacked at the tunnel mouth. A maintenance electrician arrived at 11:34, opened the drive cabinet beside the entry belt, and noted a warm smell. While Screening Lines 1 and 2 remained in service, bags from check-in desks 40 to 62 were redirected to lower-capacity Line 2. The security screening hall was closed to non-staff from 11:40 until the line was cleared, and passengers on two delayed flights were asked to remain near check-in until bag status was confirmed. Security personnel hand re-screened bags during the stoppage using a manual procedure for software-flagged items. Line 3 remained fully out of service until being cleared for normal throughput at 14:40. Ground handling ramp dispatch recorded four departures with delayed baggage loading, two extra loaders at the screened-bag chute, and a final affected flight pushback at 15:12.

Sources: Tessarine Bay Airport Security Operations Desk Log, Tessarine Bay Airport Baggage Control Room Log, Screening Line 3 Drive Controller Event Record, Tessarine Bay Airport Screening Hall Supervisor Odalys Merrin's statement, Marlen Ground Handling Ramp Dispatch Sheet

On a Thursday in May at 1:26 p.m., the freight elevator in the Finishing Building of the Lindqvist Textile Mill stopped between the second and third floors while travelling upward. The controller log recorded a stop command from the safety circuit at that moment, and the car's load cell registered 1,140 kilograms, within the unit's rated capacity of 1,500 kilograms. Teodor Bram, the cart operator, was inside the car with a cart of fabric bolts. He used the in-car call button to reach the security desk by intercom, which logged the call at 1:27 p.m. No injuries were reported.

The available records give conflicting accounts of the cause. The maintenance work order attributes the stop solely to the overspeed governor tripping on the upward run. The elevator technician, Dorrel Vance, attributes it solely to a worn door interlock contact on the third-floor landing door. This discrepancy must be resolved before corrective action is closed out. The work order also notes that the last scheduled inspection was in March.

Vance signed in at the security gate at 1:48 p.m., proceeded to the roof machine room, and isolated the main power supply. He then lowered the car by manually releasing the brake in short steps until it reached the second-floor landing, where Bram exited. Estimates of how long the car was stranded differ: Bram reported about 25 minutes, while the security desk log recorded about 40 minutes. The elevator was tagged out of service until the following morning. The controller log shows the safety circuit reset after power was restored at 8:05 a.m. the next day. Imogen Pask, the finishing floor supervisor, arranged for the remaining fabric bolts to be moved to the third floor by stairs and the small passenger lift.

Sources: Teodor Bram, Lindqvist Mill Elevator Controller Event Log, Imogen Pask, Lindqvist Mill Maintenance Work Order, Dorrel Vance, Lindqvist Mill Security Desk Log

The incident occurred at Harnsey Fish Works on Lantern Quay in Thornwick Sands at about 1:50 a.m. on a Thursday in July, when a gas leak was detected in Cold Store 2. The fixed ammonia-propane detector panel in that cold store registered its first high-level alarm at 1:48 a.m., and its peak reading reached 38 percent of the lower explosive limit. The plant reported a suspected gas leak to the Gas Board at 1:56 a.m. The Shift Log records 14 workers on shift in the plant when the alarm began. Night shift supervisor Odile Brandt heard the detector horn from the packing hall and ordered the cold store staff out, and she stated that nobody reported symptoms to her at the muster point beside the ice plant. The Shift Log notes that the packing hall extraction fans were switched off on Brandt's instruction.

The Thornwick Sands Fire Brigade set up a cordon on Lantern Quay extending about 60 meters from the cold store doors. Crew commander Tomas Verrill reported that his crew reached the cold store doors before the gas board engineer arrived on the quay, and that they entered the cold store wearing breathing apparatus. The gas board dispatch record shows an engineer assigned to the plant's incoming propane supply line, though Brandt reports that the engineer reached the cold store doors before the brigade crew arrived on the quay, so the sequence of arrival should be reconciled in review. The brigade crew later took readings at the cold store doorways and declared the building clear for re-entry. The detector panel's readings fell below its alarm threshold at 3:05 a.m.

Two refrigerated trucks from Rennick Haulage were waiting at the loading dock when the alarm began. The gate ledger shows both trucks leaving the quay gate before 2:20 a.m. without their loads. The loading dock stayed closed for about two to four hours after the alarm began, depending on the source. Frozen stock in Cold Store 2 was moved to Cold Store 1 later that morning.

Sources: Fixed ammonia-propane detector panel, Cold Store 2; Harnsey Fish Works Shift Log; Tomas Verrill, Thornwick Sands Fire Brigade crew commander; Thornwick Sands Gas Board Dispatch Record; Odile Brandt, night shift supervisor at Harnsey Fish Works; Rennick Haulage Gate Ledger

Grid power failed at 00:58. The standby generator started automatically about 20 seconds later and ran for 38 minutes before shutting down at 01:36, while grid supply remained unavailable. The controller recorded a stop event followed by a lockout requiring manual reset at the generator panel. The cause remains unresolved: the site engineer attributed the shutdown to overheating protection after snow blocked the cooling air intake, while the night operator attributed it to low oil pressure protection.

Reports conflict on the sequence of outages. Soller reported that the dome drive lost power before the control room lights; shift handover notes say the lights failed first. Soller observed both systems go down while battery-backed computers remained on. Renk, working in the visitor wing, reported that corridor lights went out as the generator noise faded.

The fuel gauge read 61 percent at 01:00 and 48 percent at 02:00, with no sudden drop recorded between 01:00 and 02:10. Pryce, who lived 300 metres away, walked to the site through snow in about ten minutes and reset the lockout, restarting the generator at 02:04. The telescope-control UPS was rated for about 25 minutes. The dome shutter had been closed at 00:50 ahead of the snow. The access road was closed, and the generator’s last routine test had been 11 days earlier. Soller was the only operator on duty.

Sources: Site engineer Talwen Pryce; Observatory night operator Imre Soller; Fuel tank level gauge record; Kestrel Ridge Observatory shift handover notes; Visiting astronomer Dr. Odalys Renk; Generator controller event log
